Class & Object.title: Class & Object
Class & Object.intro: A class is a blueprint that defines the data and functions an object will have. An object is an instance of a class created from that blueprint.
bullets: A class defines data members and member functions.
An object is a real instance created from a class.
Multiple objects can be created from one class.
In DataVerse, ArrayModule is a class and arrayModule is an object of that class.
Class & Object.viva: Class = blueprint; Object = instance of a class.

Encapsulation.title: Encapsulation
Encapsulation.intro: Encapsulation is the process of bundling data and the functions that operate on that data into one unit while restricting direct access to internal data.
bullets: Private data cannot be accessed directly from outside the class.
Public functions provide controlled access to the data.
It improves data safety and maintainability.
DataVerse's ArrayModule keeps its vector data private and exposes operations through public functions.
Encapsulation.visual:
OUTSIDE USER
      │
      ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│      ArrayModule       │
│                        │
│  PRIVATE: data         │
│       ▲                │
│       │ controlled     │
│       │ access         │
│  PUBLIC: display()     │
│          insert()      │
└────────────────────────┘
Encapsulation.viva: Encapsulation = data + methods together with controlled access.

Abstraction.title: Abstraction
Abstraction.intro: Abstraction means exposing the essential operation to the user while hiding the internal implementation details.
bullets: The user sees what an operation does rather than every internal step.
Implementation details remain inside the class.
It reduces complexity for the user.
In DataVerse, insertElement(position, value) hides the shifting implementation.
Abstraction.example:
arrayModule.insertElement(2, 50);

// User does not need to manually shift every element.
Abstraction.visual:
USER
  │
  │ insertElement(2,50)
  ▼
┌─────────────────────┐
│   PUBLIC INTERFACE  │
├─────────────────────┤
│ validation          │
│ create space        │
│ shift elements      │
│ insert value        │
│ update state        │
└─────────────────────┘
Abstraction.viva: Abstraction = show essential functionality, hide implementation.

Inheritance.title: Inheritance
Inheritance.intro: Inheritance is one of the fundamental concepts of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) that allows a class to acquire the properties and behaviors of another class. It promotes code reusability by enabling new classes to extend existing classes instead of rewriting code.
bullets: Allows derived classes to reuse members of an existing class.
Supports code reusability and hierarchical class design.
The existing class is called the base or parent class.
The new class is called the derived or child class.
Common forms are single, multilevel, multiple, hierarchical and hybrid inheritance.
Inheritance.viva: Inheritance = IS-A relationship and code reuse. Example: Dog IS-A Animal.

Polymorphism.title: Polymorphism
Polymorphism.intro: Polymorphism means 'many forms'. The same interface or function name can produce different behavior depending on the situation.
bullets: Compile-time polymorphism includes function overloading and operator overloading.
Runtime polymorphism commonly uses virtual functions and overriding.
It allows a common interface for different derived-class behaviors.
The original ArrayModule prototype does not explicitly implement runtime polymorphism.

Constructor & Destructor.title: Constructor & Destructor
Constructor & Destructor.intro: A constructor is a special member function that runs when an object is created. A destructor runs when the object's lifetime ends and is used for cleanup.
bullets: A constructor has the same name as the class.
A constructor has no return type.
A destructor uses ~ followed by the class name.
Constructors can initialize data members.
C++ can provide compiler-generated constructors/destructors when they are not explicitly written.
Constructor & Destructor.visual:
object created
      ↓
 CONSTRUCTOR
      ↓
 object initialized
      ↓
 object used
      ↓
 object lifetime ends
      ↓
  DESTRUCTOR

Composition.title: Composition
Composition.intro: Composition represents a HAS-A relationship in which one class contains an object of another class as a component.
bullets: The containing class is built from other objects.
It supports modular system design.
DataVerse's ExperimentManager contains an ArrayModule object.
Composition is different from inheritance: HAS-A versus IS-A.
Composition.viva: Composition = HAS-A relationship. Inheritance = IS-A relationship.

Time & Space Complexity.title: Time & Space Complexity
Time & Space Complexity.intro: Complexity measures how the running time and memory requirements of an algorithm grow as the input size increases.
bullets: Time complexity describes growth in execution steps.
Space complexity describes additional memory used.
Big-O expresses the growth rate for algorithm analysis.
Common classes include O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), and O(n²).
Time & Space Complexity.visual:
Input n grows → work grows

O(1)       ─────
O(log n)   ─────╱
O(n)       ────╱
O(n²)      ───╱╱
Time & Space Complexity.viva: Big-O focuses on growth rate rather than exact machine time.

Array.title: Array
Array.intro: An array stores elements in contiguous memory locations and provides index-based access.
bullets: Elements are accessed using indexes.
Access by index is typically O(1).
Insertion/deletion in the middle may require shifting.
Arrays are useful when fast indexed access is important.
Array.viva: Array access O(1); middle insertion/deletion generally O(n).

Linked List.title: Linked List
Linked List.intro: A linked list stores elements in nodes. Each node contains data and a link/reference to the next node.
bullets: HEAD points to the first node.
Each node stores DATA and NEXT.
The last node points to NULL.
Nodes do not need to be contiguous in memory.
Insertion/deletion can be efficient when the required node/reference is known.
Linked List.viva: Linked list = nodes connected by links; traversal/search O(n).

Stack.title: Stack
Stack.intro: A stack is a linear data structure that follows LIFO: Last In, First Out.
bullets: Push inserts an element at TOP.
Pop removes the element at TOP.
Peek reads TOP without removing it.
Display shows the current stack.
Stack can be implemented using an array or linked list.
Stack.viva: Stack = LIFO. Push, Pop and Peek are typically O(1).

Queue.title: Queue
Queue.intro: A queue is a linear data structure that follows FIFO: First In, First Out.
bullets: Enqueue inserts at REAR.
Dequeue removes from FRONT.
Front/Peek reads the first element.
Queues model waiting lines and scheduling systems.
A queue can be implemented using arrays or linked lists.
Queue.viva: Queue = FIFO. With a suitable implementation enqueue/dequeue can be O(1).

Binary Tree / BST.title: Binary Tree / Binary Search Tree
Binary Tree / BST.intro: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children. A Binary Search Tree (BST) maintains an ordering rule.
bullets: Each node can have a left and right child.
In a BST, smaller values go left and larger values go right.
Inorder traversal of a BST produces sorted order.
Common traversals are inorder, preorder and postorder.
Binary Tree / BST.viva: Balanced BST search/insert/delete is O(log n) average; worst case O(n).

Graph.title: Graph
Graph.intro: A graph is a non-linear data structure made of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections).
bullets: Vertices represent entities or points.
Edges represent relationships/connections.
Graphs can be directed or undirected.
BFS explores level by level using a queue.
DFS explores deeply using recursion or a stack.
Graph.viva: BFS/DFS are O(V + E) with an adjacency-list representation.

Hashing.title: Hashing
Hashing.intro: Hashing maps a key to a location in a hash table using a hash function.
bullets: The hash function converts a key into an index/bucket.
A collision occurs when multiple keys map to the same bucket.
Chaining stores multiple entries in a bucket.
A good hash function distributes keys across the table.
Hashing.viva: Hashing average search/insert/delete O(1); worst case can be O(n).

Searching.title: Searching
Searching.intro: Searching is the process of finding whether a target value exists in a data structure and locating its position.
bullets: Linear search checks elements one by one.
Binary search repeatedly divides a sorted range.
Binary search requires sorted data.
The DataVerse visualizer shows pointer/range decisions.
Searching.example:
Sorted: 10 20 30 40 50
Target: 40

low=0, high=4, mid=2 → 30
Target is larger → move low
Searching.viva: Linear search O(n); binary search O(log n) on sorted data.

Sorting.title: Sorting
Sorting.intro: Sorting rearranges elements into a chosen order, such as ascending or descending order.
bullets: Bubble sort compares adjacent elements and swaps them when needed.
Selection sort repeatedly selects the minimum/maximum.
Insertion sort inserts each element into its correct earlier position.
Merge sort divides the data, sorts subarrays and merges them.
Sorting.viva: Bubble/Selection/Insertion are typically O(n²); Merge sort O(n log n).
